Old age and death— these are the ten stages of the mind-born god [Kāma] for women and men whose hearts are agitated by passion.
Having observed the gestures of women, the wise man proceeds;
indeed, he attains the state of being beloved by slender-waisted women. (MinSd 174)
A wise man should accomplish what is to be achieved through effort and indeed through speech;
for women, the means of accomplishment are difficult, and they are hard to fathom.
The exposure of the armpits, the base of the arms, the sides, the belly, and the breasts; likewise, the release of the young woman’s embrace and the loosening of her braid of hair.
The constant gazing at one's own limbs, the shedding of tears, the rubbing of fingers, and the frequent discharge of phlegm; (MinSd 177)
The proclamation of one's beloved’s excellence in beauty, fortune, playfulness, and virtues; great exultation; and the crushing of one’s own limbs [with joy]. (MinSd 178)
The casting of fingers along the path of the ears, and the glancing of the eyes at the face with a smile—
one should recognize these as signs that indicate the goal cannot be accomplished.

A woman adorned with modesty, lovely, free from passion, and devoid of greed is one who can be accomplished; she possesses the power of the meaning of the *liṅga*. She is proclaimed to be one who is not [easily] accomplished.
One who speaks well is won with effort; one who is destitute of wealth is won by living abroad;
a wife whose gestures are contrary to her intentions is won with effort; likewise, a housewife is won with effort. (MinSd 181)
In gardens, festivals, and sacred fords; on roads, in enclosures, and in forests; in the company of undesirable women, in a field, and likewise in the house of one's father.
In a temple, in a hut, as well as while frequenting ponds and the like,
during dancing, in a cow-pen, and likewise at the festivals of kinsmen’s houses—
women must always be protected by the virtuous through their own diligent effort.
A young woman must always be protected with truthful gifts and sweet words;
for if she is not protected, she will surely bring about the ruin of the family through her attachment to outsiders.
One who is elegantly adorned, wise, pure, prosperous, a singer, and skilled in entering convivial gatherings— such a person is considered a *nāgara* (urbane man) possessing six qualities.
One who is generous, discerning, skillful, of noble birth, proficient in the arts, wise, wealthy,
capable in worldly affairs, all-enduring, happy, illustrious, and of excellent character— he indeed shall be the leader.
A washerwoman, a garland-maker, a nurse, a female ascetic, a neighbor, a female friend, a cowherd’s wife, a maidservant, a barber’s wife, a widow, and an actress. (MinSd 187)
She is considered to be a maidservant, a young girl, an astrologer, and a female messenger;
she wears diverse ornaments, is skillful, and understands the gestures of others.
A female messenger is considered to be proficient, of steady disposition, and bold;
she is appointed to the task as one adorned with eloquence in many languages.
She whose anger corresponds to her resentment, yet who is satisfied when conciliated,
is clearly perceived as one whose mind is captivated by the virtues of her lord.
Day after day, full of passion, she sends a female messenger and hastens eagerly to some place of appointment;
yet, by the turn of fate, her lover does not appear—Bharata declares such a heroine to be "deceived" (*vipralabdhā*).
She whose husband, drawn by the qualities of her pleasure, does not leave her side,
and who is intent on various amorous dalliances, is one who has her husband under her own control.

She who, having become single-minded, constantly meditates upon the separation from her beloved and the graceful gestures of her lover's beauty, is considered to be a woman suffering from the pangs of separation.
Trembling with the fever of the unbridled arrows of Love, bearing auspicious flowers upon her ears amidst horripilation,
she who proceeds fearlessly for the sake of union with her beloved is indeed a heroine known as an *abhisārikā*.
She who, rendered shameless by intense intoxication and passion,
goes out to meet her beloved, is called an *abhisārikā* by the wise.
She whose beloved, though accustomed to her, has failed to go to the rendezvous due to ignorance,
and who is tormented by his non-arrival, is celebrated as a *khaṇḍitā*.
A beloved husband who has been rejected by anger, yet remains capable [of returning],
while she herself persists in her resentment without him, is described by the wise as "the angry woman" (kupitā).
She is the *vāsakasajjā* (one adorned for the tryst) who, having ascertained through a female messenger that her husband will arrive at a secluded place, remains intent on watching the door.
Having encountered the irresistible and terrible union with the god of love, her mind agitated and overwhelmed,
trembling from the fever of the unassailable arrows of Manmatha, Bharata, the lord of poets, describes her as thus longing.
The *priyā* (beloved) moves alone, the *uṣṇā* (hot) runs, and likewise the *unmādinī* (mad) [runs];
when the beloved remains right there, she is considered *virahotkaṇṭhitā* (longing in separation).

The successful accomplishment of what is difficult to achieve and the winning over of what is achievable proceed perfectly according to one's own will; this is the proper purpose of the science of love (*kāmaśāstra*).
Then, whether it be pure or impure, once its ritual action has been mastered and the mantra obtained from the mouth of the Guru, it is accomplished here; of this there is no doubt.
Then the word *tricāmuṇḍe* is recited, followed by *kvanu kvanu*; then the word *chanu chanu*, which brings [the target] under one's own control.
Having provided the name of the person to be accomplished in the accusative case, one should join it with "svāhā.
By generally performing the recitation of the name of such-and-such a person, one shall bring them under control.
With the mantra "hrīṃ svāhā," conjoined with the name of the person to be accomplished, one should consecrate a flower seven times; whoever takes that flower shall be brought under control.
By anointing with the tongue of a crow, the wing of a bee, golden excrement, and tears,
as well as blood from the organ of passion, wise men may bring others under their control.
The seed-syllable of speech born of enjoyment, and the tongue as a white arka petal—
having ground these together, one who has anointed their eyes with them can bring even a wife under control.
Having ground together yellow orpiment, realgar, and red sandalwood, if this is applied with a flower upon the head of anyone, she becomes as submissive as a beast.
Having ground the heart of an owl together with saffron, one should make a *tilaka* mark; by that, the world becomes submissive. (MinSd 208)
Aśvagandhā, vacā, kuṣṭha, balā, and likewise nāgabalā,
along with buffalo butter and combined with gajapippalī.
Having ground them together with goat’s urine, the application of the resulting paste from *śūkaśimbī* is the supreme means for making [the body] firm. (MinSd 210)
Surely by applying its paste, the penis becomes like iron;
blue lotus, white lotus, filaments, honey, and sugar [are the ingredients].
By smearing the navel with these, a lover enjoys for a long time;
having ground a lotus in milk, water is made into a pill.
One should place the bone of a black cat, obtained from its right side, either in the lap or somewhere scattered about.
The seed of the *saptaparṇa* tree, when bound around the waist, certainly causes constipation;
indeed, it arrests one's own semen.
Holding in one's hand the root of the white *śarapuṃkhā* together with mercury,
with a *karañja* seed placed in the middle, one should bind the seed along with its root.
Kusumbha oil, processed with the roots of the ketakī plant, bhūmilatā, and asanā,
certainly brings about the immobilization of the seed (semen) in men when applied as an ointment to the soles of the feet.
A powder made from buffalo curd, *sahadevī*, sesame, honey, and the white filaments of the lotus,
when mixed and applied as an ointment to the navel, certainly causes the retention of semen.
Mercury placed within the seed of *bṛhatkarañja* and wrapped in lotus petals—this seed, when cast into the mouth, certainly brings about paralysis. (MinSd 218)
One should first perform the cutting and, especially, the crushing;
then one should soak the husked and split *māṣa* beans for seven days.
Then, one should again perform the visualization of them with coconut water;
after that, one should consume [the substance] prepared with milk, which has fallen from thick clouds.
Then, full of desire, he lusts after hundreds of thousands of women.
But he who, having bent his foot, should apply the sandal with the *samāna* [vāyu], and being composed, should press it against the ground with the big toe; MinSd_222.
Alternatively, one may consume [the powder] burnt together with *campaka* and plantain;
when combined with the very tips [of these], it bestows prosperity once again.
One whose mental activity is fixed upon lotus ponds, groves, mountain caves, and other such sources of pleasure,
and who possesses unshakable fortitude, enjoys for a long time even when relaxed, in a state of intense and uninterrupted delight.
Mercury, ṭaṅkaṇa salt, the three pungents (vyoṣa), kākamācī, and honey—
by using these, a lover whose penis remains erect for a long time shall always delight his woman.
One should apply an ointment made of equal parts of *tumbī* leaf and *lodhra*.
When this is applied to the vulva, even one who has given birth remains unhurt.
Oil produced from the flowers of the *palāśa* and *udumbara* trees, when applied to the vagina with honey, is the best means for making it firm. (MinSd 227)
The mantra of one's own chosen deity is recited for one's own sake without violence;
indeed, one remains established in celibacy while giving gifts according to one's prosperity.
Having first performed purification there, one should again [act] in the field during an auspicious aspect,
especially at sunrise or at dusk, for then one is personally powerful.
And having become single-minded, if the wise man releases the seed,
he will surely give birth at the end of the month to one who is virtuous and renowned.
